results.note: Header 'Review'; Methods give measurement only, no search or criteria; reference list (pp. 9-11): Greenwald first author 2002/2003/2007, second author of Zubieta 2000 ('male' in title, p. 11); Comer first author 2005; conclusion p. 1.

results.corrected_extracted: The authors use receptor availability (non-displaceable binding potential), an indirect measure, instead of 'occupancy', which they call misleading and not measurable directly in people except with extraordinary methods (to obtain receptor concentration and affinity); if receptor affinity and endogenous opioid levels are assumed constant, a fall in availability is proportional to a rise in occupancy. Measures taken 4 hours after the daily dose, the earliest post-dose time studied, probably reflect less than the largest fall in availability; within-day PET time courses are not feasible. There is no gold-standard definition of clinically meaningful blockade, and neither the availability needed for withdrawal suppression or blockade nor how it varies with patients, opioids and routes is known.
results.note: Wording only, no number changes: source says occupancy cannot be measured directly 'except with extraordinary methods', and gives proportionality under an assumption ('If we assume'), not as 'only if'. Rest confirmed at 2.1.1 and 2.2.1.

results.corrected_extracted: The studies reviewed enrolled people dependent on heroin who were not seeking treatment and who usually kept using between inpatient stays; the authors call generalizability to people dependent on other opioids, such as oxycodone or hydrocodone, or seeking treatment unclear. Ages were limited to 18–50; many fewer women than men took part, and the small samples gave too little statistical power to examine gender or age; people with substance use disorders other than nicotine, depressive, psychotic or anxiety disorders, pregnancy or medical conditions such as active hepatitis were excluded, and the authors say these relatively healthy volunteers do not represent patients in clinical practice. All imaging used a buprenorphine-only product; the authors cite data suggesting that buprenorphine and buprenorphine/naloxone products under the tongue have similar effects.
results.note: Hedge restored: 'data suggest' similar effects (Strain et al., 2000). Inadequate power is put down to small samples in general, not only to the few women. Paragraph locators and all other facts confirmed.

results.corrected_extracted: The authors lack longitudinal follow-up of people with these lesions: only one included series (Trimarchi et al., 2003) gives some sparse information on progression over time, which they say seems to confirm their hypothesis; the order of spread (septum, then the lower third, then the middle third, then the skull base or lamina papyracea) is a hypothesis drawn from the decreasing counts, which needs prospective validation; one-sided use, septal deviation before use and the effect of substances mixed into cocaine could not be accounted for. The authors suggest that the lack of follow-up may be partly due to stigmatization (people with these lesions tend to seek care late and often perceive a request to stop cocaine as a moral judgment, citing one paper), which they say correlates with a high rate of loss to follow-up. The conclusion calls for prospective studies following the evolution of the lesions. Table 3 gives no use status for the 2003 series.
results.note: Hedge restored: the lack of follow-up 'may be partially due to' stigmatization, which the original left out; late presentation and loss to follow-up are given as its consequences. Rest confirmed (Discussion paras 6-7, Conclusion, Table 3).

Few series gave solid data, and the authors say their analysis seems to suggest that no relationship can be drawn between the lesions inside the nose and the extent of external nose involvement.
results.note: Table 5 also lists a nasal ala fistula with dorsum-ala collapse (n=1, Colletti et al. [4]), which the count omitted. The no-relationship finding is hedged in the source ('seems to suggest'; few articles with solid data). Other counts confirmed.

results.corrected_extracted: Amphetamine screens: the energy supplement DMAA gave false positives on two laboratory assays, in spiked urine and in the urine of people taking it; three women prescribed labetalol screened positive and GC-MS found no amphetamines; metformin in a case report (one point-of-care test); promethazine (3 specimens) and chlorpromazine (6) were positive on one assay and negative by LC-PDA, and on retesting all 9 were negative on two other kits while 2 were positive on a third; trazodone added to drug-free urine gave false positives on one ecstasy (MDMA) screen but not on the same maker's amphetamine kit, which that study's authors think most likely due to its metabolite m-CPP; m-CPP gave false positives on another amphetamine assay (trazodone itself only above 200 µg/mL), on which 3 of 6 patients taking trazodone screened positive and were negative by GC-MS; in 6 healthy men given two doses of the antibiotic ofloxacin 12 hours apart, no sample before and all 6 samples after screened positive on one amphetamine assay, the lowest almost four times the 300 ng/mL cutoff.

results.corrected_extracted: In a retrospective chart review of amphetamine screens (Syva EMIT II Plus) that GC-MS did not confirm, 41% of the samples (printed in words; 53 patients) came from patients taking bupropion at the time; after statistically ruling out polysubstance use as a cause, the investigators are said to have concluded that a large portion of these false positives stemmed directly from bupropion; no spiking experiment showed that bupropion or its metabolites caused the result, which the authors call an important limitation. The total number of unconfirmed screens and the share of people taking bupropion who screened positive are not given. Editors' arithmetic: about 129 unconfirmed screens if 53 is 41%.
results.note: Source: 'statistically ruling out poly-substance abuse as a cause', not ruling out use of other substances; the investigators' conclusion is added. 41%/53, Table I assay and 53/0.41 ≈ 129 confirmed.

results.corrected_extracted: Cannabis (THC) screens: urine of patients taking efavirenz screened positive on three immunoassays (cutoff 50 µg/L), an interference attributed to its glucuronide metabolite (efavirenz and 8-OH efavirenz were found not to interfere); in another study, Rapid Response test strips were positive in 28 of 30 patients taking efavirenz for at least 2 weeks, while the other point-of-care device and two automated immunoassays were negative; in 5 volunteers taking the anti-inflammatory niflumic acid, all 55 urine samples were positive on Roche KIMS and negative on Syva EMIT; four commercial baby soaps gave positives on the Vitros THC immunoassay at a 20 ng/mL cutoff; ibuprofen and naproxen are listed as case reports with the Syva EMIT d.a.u. cannabinoid assay (cutoff 20 µg/L) and with the Abbott TDx barbiturate assay (Table VI).

results.corrected_extracted: PCP screens: because PCP use is rare and PCP immunoassays are not specific, the positive predictive value of a PCP screen is very low. Venlafaxine: after an overdose, one assay was positive for PCP and GC-MS negative; in three other patients taking venlafaxine, one point-of-care test was positive at a 25 ng/mL cutoff while three other PCP assays and GC-MS were negative. Tramadol: false positives with negative GC-MS in two patients who had taken large overdoses (one assay), with tramadol and N-desmethyltramadol each triggering that assay in spiked urine, and in two further overdose patients on another assay. MDPV ('bath salts') in spiked urine gave false-positive PCP results on one assay, after a patient's apparent overdose with no PCP found; lamotrigine in a case report. LSD screens cross-reacted with many medicines on one assay (EMIT II LSD), among them amitriptyline, bupropion, fluoxetine, haloperidol, risperidone, sertraline and trazodone; the mucus-thinning medicine ambroxol caused unexpected LSD positives in twelve patients (the review does not name the assay) and also cross-reacts significantly with the CEDIA DAU LSD assay (spiked urine in Table VI).
results.note: The text (p. 8) does not say on which assay the twelve patients tested positive; CEDIA DAU LSD appears only as an additional cross-reactivity ('also exhibits'; Table VI: spiking). Rest confirmed, Misc paras 1-5.

They note, citing a placebo-controlled trial, that comparison with baseline may understate a drug's adverse effects, adding that this would not affect the comparison of the two drugs; ratings were mostly in the mild range of the 0 to 9 scale; and only moderate doses given twice a day were studied, so other doses and spacing might give different side-effect profiles.

results.corrected_extracted: Table 3, stated to be modified from the author's own 1998 paper, lists eight single-dose study arms of a benzodiazepine with alcohol: benzodiazepine metabolism 'unchanged' in five (alprazolam 0.5 and 2 mg by mouth with ethanol 0.8 g/kg, by plasma concentration; diazepam 5 mg with 48 g; diazepam 10 mg with 0.8 g/kg drunk 3 hours after the diazepam; diazepam 10 mg with an intravenous ethanol infusion; triazolam 0.5 mg with 25 g), 'decreased' in two (brotizolam 0.25 mg with 24 g: Cmax, half-life and clearance; diazepam 10 mg with 0.8 g/kg: plasma concentration) and 'increased' in one (triazolam 0.5 mg with an ethanol 'loading' regimen, which the footnote, ambiguously worded, describes as oral ethanol for 7.5 hours starting 1 hour before, holding breath concentrations at 800–950 mg/L: area under the curve, mean 21%); doses are the studies' conditions. The column is headed 'Benzodiazepine Metabolism' with the measure in brackets, so for the three changed arms it is not stated whether the word refers to metabolism or to the measure. The abstract says that metabolism is in general delayed with acute alcohol, although some reports suggest otherwise; the text cites an older review (Sellers and Busto, 1982) as finding benzodiazepine concentrations raised in most cases.
results.note: Only change: footnote c does not say the loading came before triazolam ('Before 1 hour, ethanol was administered for 7.5 hour' to hold breath 800-950 mg/L). All rows, refs 2 and 3 and the abstract confirmed on renderings.

results.corrected_extracted: Table 4 lists fatal poisonings with both ethanol and benzodiazepines in the blood, described as cases reported from 1988 to the present, with no total and no count of people who took both and lived. Editors' count of the rows: 39 deaths from 10 reports (references 49–58, published 1988–1999), 25 of them from one Canadian forensic series of triazolam cases (Joynt, 1993; footnoted as covering only deaths due to drugs and drug-related deaths); 32 rows name triazolam; blood ethanol 0.1–3.2 mg/mL (editors' median 1.7); triazolam at or below 20 ng/mL, the top of the therapeutic range the table quotes from one case report (reference 55), in 13 of the 32, counting one trace; alprazolam in 3 rows, each with other substances (200 ng/mL with triazolam and others; a trace with triazolam, diazepam and nordiazepam; 210 ng/mL with others, in a report titled as a fatal overdose of tramadol and alprazolam). The text states, without a count, that fatal poisoning appears to occur more often with ethanol and several benzodiazepines than with one, adding that an excess total amount of benzodiazepines must also be considered, and puts the many triazolam reports down, probably, to its lower therapeutic concentration.
results.note: Only 'probably' restored (p. 73). Counts recomputed on the 300-dpi Table 4: 39 rows, 10 reports, 25 Joynt, 32 triazolam, 13 at or below 20 ng/mL, median 1.7; one stray age '48' with no values, rightly not counted.

key_findings.correction: In the authors' summary of earlier human studies, buprenorphine brought on moderate to severe withdrawal in people maintained on methadone 60 mg/day, and less in people on methadone 25–30 mg/day or on heroin; citing animal and human studies, the review says that whether it precipitates withdrawal depends on the level of dependence, the opioid depended on, and the time since its last dose. (The dependence sentence is not limited to animal studies: it cites Kosten and Kleber, 1988, and Walsh et al., 1995a, human studies by their titles, as well as Sell et al., 2003, and Woods' animal work.)

Finding unchanged and confirmed; note corrected to: Availability is the share of receptors still free to bind the tracer; the authors treat a fall in availability as proportional to a rise in occupancy if receptor affinity and endogenous opioid levels are assumed constant (2.1.1, PDF p. 3). The legend of Fig. 1 gives 12–33% for 8 mg/day, against 20–35% in Table 1 (see reporting issues). (The source says 'proportional', under an assumption, not 'equate ... only if'.)

reporting_issues.correction: issue: Table 1, note b, says that values for doses not studied are in italics, but no value in Table 1 is italicized (checked on the page rendered at 300 dpi); only the text and the data points of Fig. 1 (left panel) show that 2, 16 and 32 mg/day were studied. The 1 mg/day estimate lies below the studied range (2–32 mg/day), and the text calls the range of estimates 16-fold although the table spans 1 to 32 mg/day. | consequence: Curve-fit estimates (1, 4, 8, 12 and 24 mg/day) can be mistaken for measurements; the 1 mg/day value is an extrapolation.

risk_of_bias.note: Narrative review, no applicable instrument; overall high and the five domains are supported by the PDF (no search; authors' own studies; abstract states thresholds the Summary calls preliminary).

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial: abstract gives thresholds and dose translations as results; 2.2.1 says the thresholds are unknown and 4.3 says blockade not reliably observed and the 20% figure is preliminary modelling.

missed: outcomes.validity_norms says a fall in availability 'equals' a rise in occupancy 'only if' affinity and endogenous levels stay constant, and that occupancy 'cannot be measured directly in humans'; the source (2.1.1, PDF p. 3) says 'proportional', under an assumption, and adds 'except with extraordinary methods' (receptor concentration and affinity).

Source inconsistency not flagged: 2.2.3, 7th paragraph (PDF p. 4) says all imaging studies used a BUP-mono tablet, but Results, 1st paragraph (p. 4) says Zubieta et al. (2000) used the liquid formulation; sample.selection_effects repeats 'tablet' while the card's exposure field says liquid.

Results, 7th paragraph (PDF p. 5) and Fig. 3 upper left (p. 6): in the 2003 study, availability related to withdrawal and craving but the effects were 'clinically modest' (<50% of maximum effect); in the figure withdrawal stays below about 30% of maximum even at placebo (read from the plot), which bears on the ≤50% withdrawal-suppression threshold.

key_findings.correction: Cocaine use was rarely described: some figure for duration in 11 of 17 series (2 to 30 years where given), frequency in 2, and continuing or stopped use in 8 series (editors' count from Table 3: 33 people, 18 continuing and 15 stopped); levamisole exposure in one study. The authors judge these data too sparse for any solid conclusion, let alone for relating use to the pattern of damage. (Counts recomputed and confirmed; 'solid' restored from p. 3265.)

The review lacks longitudinal follow-up data: by its account only Trimarchi et al. (2003) gave sparse information on progression, which the authors say seems to confirm their hypothesis. The order of spread (septum, then lower and side walls, then ethmoid, then orbit or skull base) is the authors' hypothesis from the site shares, which they say needs prospective validation; the review reports no data on what happened to lesions after people stopped using cocaine. (The source does not say that no series reported this; it reports none. See 'missed' on Trimarchi et al., 2001.)

Surgical pathology, reported for some series, was mostly nonspecific: chronic inflammation, fibrosis or necrosis, with vasculitis-like changes (microabscesses in venule walls, leukocytoclastic vasculitis, thrombi) in two of the three Trimarchi series (2001 and 2003; Table 6 gives nonspecific findings for the 2017 series) and features suggesting IgG4 disease in one series. Histology could not be related to lesion extent or site.

reporting_issues.correction: issue: Several counts in Table 6 exceed the number of people with CIMDL in the series: Subesinghe et al., 11 (6 people with CIMDL among 14); Trimarchi et al. 2001, 19, 24 and 25 (18 people); Trimarchi et al. 2003, 27 (25 people). The primary paper of Trimarchi et al. (2001) shows its figures are counts of biopsies (44 biopsies from 18 people), which the table does not say. | consequence: Table 6 mixes biopsy counts with patient counts; its numbers cannot be read as numbers of people. (The 2003 count of 22 does not exceed 25; 44 biopsies checked in the 2001 PDF.)

risk_of_bias.note: AMSTAR 2 critically low holds: items 7 (no excluded-studies list; Fig. 1 counts only, 173 = 15+7+7+25+3+112+4) and 13 fail; item 4's 'no' follows the project's reading (8 language exclusions confirmed in Fig. 1). Wilson intervals recomputed: identical.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial. In point (4), keep the source's hedge: the lack of follow-up 'may be partially due to' stigmatization, with late presentation and loss to follow-up given as its consequences (p. 3265).

missed: analysis.effect_sizes lists the external-nose single cases as nostrils, nasal ala, columella and philtrum, omitting the nasal ala fistula with collapse of the dorsum-ala complex (n=1) in Colletti et al., 2014 (Table 5, p. 3264); the philtrum case is Marí et al.'s saddle nose.

The review says only Trimarchi et al. (2003) gives longitudinal information (p. 3265), but the included Trimarchi et al. (2001) series reports follow-up imaging in 4 people, all still using cocaine, all with progressive erosion (primary paper, p. 396, in the senior author's files); with RI 5, this bears on KF 6 and on the progression hypothesis.

key_findings.correction: Trazodone added to drug-free urine gave false positives on the EMIT II Plus Ecstasy (MDMA) assay but not on the EMIT II Plus amphetamine kit (3.0 µg/mL of trazodone in the text; Table I prints 3 µg/mL as m-CPP); the study's authors think this most likely due to its metabolite m-CPP. On the Roche Amphetamines II assay, m-CPP at 6.7 µg/mL or more gave positives while trazodone itself would need over 200 µg/mL; three of six patients with trazodone above 1.0 µg/mL and serum m-CPP above 0.85 µg/mL screened positive for amphetamines and were negative by GC-MS. (Hedge from p. 3 restored; text and Table I disagree on which compound the 3 µg/mL refers to.)

Cannabis (THC) screens and efavirenz: urine of patients taking efavirenz screened positive on three immunoassays (Microgenics CEDIA DAU Multi-Level THC, Biosite Triage TOX Drug Screen, Immunalysis Direct ELISA; cutoff 50 µg/L), an interference attributed to its glucuronide metabolite (efavirenz and 8-OH efavirenz were found not to interfere); in another study, Rapid Response test strips were positive in 28 of 30 patients taking efavirenz for at least 2 weeks, while the other point-of-care device (THC One Step Marijuana) and two automated immunoassays (Roche Cannabinoids II, Beckman SYNCHRON THC2) were negative. (The source says the interference 'has been attributed to' the glucuronide, p. 4.)

Same finding, with one change: 'and ofloxacin did so in case reports' becomes 'and ofloxacin did so in a case report (fluorescence immunoassay for opiates, Triage and Multi-5; Table V, ref. 37)'. Table V lists one ofloxacin case report; its other opiate entry (EMIT II opiates, ref. 38) is spiking.

LSD screens cross-react with many drugs, most notably on the EMIT II LSD assay (amitriptyline, benzphetamine, bupropion, buspirone, cephradine, chlorpromazine, desipramine, diltiazem, doxepin, fentanyl, fluoxetine, haloperidol, imipramine, labetalol, metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, risperidone, sertraline, thioridazine, trazodone and verapamil; also ergonovine, lysergol, brompheniramine, imipramine and methylphenidate at 4,000-50,000 ng/mL); the mucolytic ambroxol caused unexpected LSD positives in 12 patients (assay not named in the review) and also cross-reacts significantly with the CEDIA DAU LSD assay (spiked urine, Table VI); fentanyl (40 µg/L; CEDIA LSD and Emit II LSD assays) and sertraline (1.5 µg/mL; CEDIA LSD) triggered LSD assays in spiked urine.

reporting_issues.note: This review's side confirmed (p. 4: Drug Screen Multi 5 negative on the presumptive positives; Blank et al., 2009, ref. 19); the Moeller et al. (2017) statement is in another source and was not checked here.

risk_of_bias.note: Narrative review, no applicable instrument; some concerns overall is fair (explicit but narrow search, no duplicate screening, evidence type labelled per entry); acknowledgment of J. A. Stone and her authorship of ref. 53 confirmed.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor: 'inclusive'/'comprehensive' against a narrow search, and 'majority ... unknown' without data; the presumptive-until-confirmed conclusion follows. The results_show examples (1 of 4, 2 of 4, 2 of 3) recounted and confirmed.

missed: exposure.polysubstance says the bupropion investigators 'ruled out use of other drugs statistically'; the source says they statistically ruled out polysubstance use as a cause of the false positives (p. 2), which is different.

Reporting issue not listed: for trazodone on the EMIT II Plus Ecstasy assay, the text gives 3.0 µg/mL of trazodone (p. 3) while Table I prints 3 µg/mL as m-CPP; which compound the threshold refers to cannot be settled from the review.

key_findings.correction: Compared with baseline, trouble sleeping (mean 3.61 vs 2.21) and poor appetite (2.74 vs 1.22) were rated more severe on dexamphetamine, and only poor appetite (2.12 vs 1.22) on methylphenidate; eight other items were rated less severe on methylphenidate than at baseline and five on dexamphetamine. (Numbers confirmed; 'increased'/'lowered' replaced: these are before-after contrasts without placebo, and the source reports higher ratings at baseline, not that the drugs lowered them.)

Same finding with one change: 'both then took methylphenidate without problems' becomes 'both tolerated methylphenidate without problems'. The source gives no order (the drug order was randomized), only that both tolerated MPH.

Parents rated most children as improved overall compared with their usual selves: 86 (68.8%) on dexamphetamine and 90 (72%) on methylphenidate; beyond a statement, without figures, that teacher and parent Conners ratings generally corroborated these proportions, the paper does not report efficacy, and it does not test this difference.

Severity ratings were generally in the mild range of the 0-to-9 scale. The authors set the 1.6% per drug who could not tolerate it beside 3.6% and 1.9% in two earlier placebo-controlled methylphenidate trials, and cite Ahmann et al.: side effects also fell from baseline on placebo, so comparison with baseline may understate a drug's adverse effects; they add that this would not affect the comparison of the two drugs with each other.

risk_of_bias.note: RoB 2 some concerns for the randomized DEX-versus-MPH contrast; the domain notes match the PDF (no sequence or concealment details, period effects unreported, df 2,122). Editors' 0.49 points and 0.31 pooled SD recomputed: correct.

interpretation_gap.note: I would rate it substantial, not minor. The abstract's conclusion that pre-existing complaints 'improve with stimulant treatment', and its statements that the drugs caused appetite loss and insomnia, rest on before-after contrasts without placebo that the Discussion partly attributes to rating artefacts.

key_findings.correction: Finding unchanged and confirmed; note corrected to: The review suggests, with a hedge ('It appears ... may be induced', p. 73), that CYP2E1 induction gives drugs metabolized by demethylation and hydroxylation an increased clearance, although it states on p. 70 that benzodiazepine metabolism is not catalysed by CYP2E1; the two human studies are from one group in 1975 (references 46 and 47).

Table 4 lists fatal poisonings in which blood held both alcohol and one or more benzodiazepines, described in the text as the cases reported from 1988 to the present. Editors' count of the printed rows: 39 deaths drawn from 10 source reports (references 49–58); 25 of the 39 rows come from a single Canadian forensic series (Joynt, 1993); 32 rows name triazolam; 14 involved more than one benzodiazepine, and 10 rows list unspecified other substances (6 of those 14 and 4 more); 16 women, 21 men, sex not printed in 2. (Was: 11 source reports; '10 more list unspecified others'.)

Triazolam concentrations in those deaths were often at or below the top of the therapeutic range the table quotes (2–20 ng/mL). Editors' count of the printed rows: of the 32 rows naming triazolam, 13 were at or below 20 ng/mL, counting the one printed as a trace, and 19 above it; in the 19 rows where triazolam is the only substance listed, 6 had triazolam at or below 20 ng/mL and the median ethanol was 1.9 mg/mL. (The original first sentence generalized to 'benzodiazepine concentrations'; other drugs were often above their quoted ranges, e.g. alprazolam 200 and 210 ng/mL against 5–20, flurazepam 50 and 200 against 5–10.)

reporting_issues.correction: issue: The abstract states that in general metabolism of these drugs is delayed when combined with acute alcohol ingestion although some reports suggest otherwise, but the review's own Table 3 shows five of eight arms unchanged; the column is headed 'Benzodiazepine Metabolism' with the parameter in brackets, so whether 'decreased' (two arms) and 'increased' (one arm, triazolam AUC, mean 21%) describe metabolism or the parameters is not stated. | consequence: The abstract's summary is not supported by the table it summarizes, and the direction of the changes cannot be read from the table. A claim should quote the table, not the abstract. (The original read 'decreased' as lower concentrations, which the table does not say.)

issue: The therapeutic ranges in the Table 4 footnote are cited to reference 55 (Uemura and Komura, 1995, a short case report, pp. 66–68, in a forensic pathology journal), not to a pharmacological compilation, and are applied to post-mortem blood without discussion of post-mortem redistribution. | consequence: Statements that a death occurred at a therapeutic concentration rest on ranges of uncertain provenance measured in a different setting from the one in which they were defined. (pp. 66–68 is three pages, not two.)

issue: Reference 51 (Wodak and Pedersen), listed in Table 4 with no age or sex, is by its title a death from combined alcohol and benzodiazepine poisoning in a non-medical detoxification unit; the review does not mention this setting, which is unlike the others in the table. | consequence: A reader counting comparable cases would need to exclude or flag it; the table treats all 39 rows alike. (The setting comes from the reference title, not from Table 4, and 'alcohol withdrawal treatment' is not stated.)

risk_of_bias.note: No instrument applies; overall high is supported (no search or criteria, no appraisal, case table from selected reports dominated by one series, no non-fatal outcomes).

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial: the respiratory-synergy sentence has no data behind it, the abstract's 'in general delayed' does not match Table 3, and 'serious problem' rests on 39 selected deaths with no denominator.

missed: design_detail and sample.recruitment say Table 4 draws on 11 source reports; it cites 10 (references 49–58), as KF 3 should also say.
sample.demographics says age is not printed in 4 rows; Table 4 prints no age in 6 rows (Wodak and Pedersen and five Joynt rows), 5 if the stray '48' belongs to the row below it.
outcomes.validity_norms says the main CYP is not determined for 12 of 24 drugs; Table 1 marks 13 as ND (as KF 9 correctly counts).

exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route says the triazolam loading regimen was '7.5 hours of oral ethanol beforehand'; footnote c reads 'Before 1 hour, ethanol was administered for 7.5 hour', which does not say the 7.5 hours preceded the triazolam.

Possible reporting issue: the three Drummer et al. (54) rows give 7-aminoflurazepam, footnoted as a flurazepam metabolite, but reference 54 is titled 'Deaths Involving the Benzodiazepine Flunitrazepam'; the drug in these deaths should be checked in the primary report before Table 4 is cited by drug.

reporting_issues.correction: issue: Principle 3 writes the bright-line rule as p below 0.05 in its first sentence and, in its last sentence (four sentences later), statistical significance as generally interpreted as p of 0.05 or less. | consequence: None for the principles; a claim quoting the conventional threshold should not depend on the difference. (Checked on the page rendered at 200 dpi: 'p < 0.05' and 'p ≤ 0.05' are four sentences apart, not two.)

risk_of_bias.note: Consensus statement, no instrument applies; 'high' only through the no-search domain, as the card explains; process facts (two dozen invited, 20 met, 3 months of drafts, 29 January 2016) and 31 acknowledged names recounted.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor: the principles are reasoning; the premise of common misuse rests on news items, a blog, Nature and Significance pieces and a journal editorial (p. 129), not on measured frequencies. 21 online commentaries recounted.
